title: my first PCB design
body:
# What I Learned Designing My First 4-Layer STM32 Bluetooth PCB

This was my first complete PCB design project. I followed the hardware design process for an STM32WB Bluetooth Low Energy board and used KiCad to go from a blank project to a board that could eventually be sent to a manufacturer. I followed the [tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nkHFoxe0mrU) on this PCB by Phil's Lab, going over two parts of the 3-part tutorial.

I learned a lot from this project, and it was my first time working towards creating a fully functioning PCB from the ground up. Each step in the PCB design process was challenging, brought up circuit fundamentals, and introduced new aspects of design to keep in mind. This took me 3 weeks, or about 5 days of work, to accomplish. 

## 1. Documentation

Before working on the schematic, I went over the MCU (microcontroller unit) [datasheet](https://www.st.com/en/microcontrollers-microprocessors/stm32wb55ce.html) of the STM32WBCE. 

I used the MCU datasheet, ST application notes, reference schematics, and component datasheets to understand things such as:

- which pins needed power
- which pins needed decoupling capacitors
- how the internal power supply circuitry worked
- what crystals were required
- how to connect the Bluetooth RF output
- what external components were recommended

This was one of the most useful lessons from the project: **the datasheet tells you what the component needs, while application notes and reference designs show you how those requirements are normally implemented.**

For example, the STM32WB has several power pins and power domains rather than one simple power input. The design tied the required supplies to 3.3 V and placed local capacitors around the MCU according to the intended power connections.

## 2. Schematic

![](/images/uploads/image-5.png)

The schematic was where the electrical design was created before worrying about the physical PCB.

I started with the STM32WB MCU and added the supporting circuitry around it. This included the power system, clocking, USB, programming/debug connections, and Bluetooth RF section.

I also learned that the schematic should communicate **design intent**. A capacitor might electrically connect between 3.3 V and ground just like several other capacitors, but it can still be intended for one specific MCU power pin. Keeping that relationship clear in the schematic makes the PCB layout much easier later.

Once the schematic was complete, I ran KiCad's **Electrical Rules Check (ERC)**. ERC checks things such as unconnected pins and incorrect electrical connections before moving on to PCB layout.

## What I've learned

### Decoupling Capacitors

A small capacitor placed next to the MCU power pin to give constant current 

Decoupling capacitors were one of the most important concepts I learned.

A microcontroller does not draw perfectly constant current. When its internal circuitry switches, it can suddenly need current for a very short period of time.

Instead of the MCU having to pull that fast burst of current through a long PCB path, it can get it from the nearby capacitor.

For this design, small 100 nF capacitors were placed close to the relevant power pins. A larger capacitor was also used as bulk decoupling near the MCU.

The PCB placement matters just as much as having the capacitor in the schematic. The tutorial emphasizes keeping the capacitor physically close to the corresponding power and ground pins so the current path stays short and low-inductance.

My simple mental model became:

**Power source → bulk capacitor → local decoupling capacitor → MCU power pin**

The closer the local capacitor is to the pin, the better it can respond to fast current changes.

## Powering the Board

The board receives power through USB.

The basic power path is:

**USB 5 V → voltage regulator → 3.3 V → MCU and other circuitry**

The regulator section is placed close to the power entry point, with input and output bypass capacitors nearby. The tutorial specifically places the regulator close to the USB power input because that is where the board's 5 V enters.

The 3.3 V rail is then distributed around the PCB using copper and vias instead of relying entirely on long, thin traces.

## Why I Used Four Layers

Before this project, I mostly thought of PCB layers as extra space for routing.

I learned that the internal layers are extremely useful electrically as well.

The board uses four copper layers approximately like this:

### Layer 1 — [F.Cu](http://F.Cu)

The top layer contains most of the components and important signal routing.

This includes connections around the MCU as well as signals such as USB and RF.

### Layer 2 — [In1.Cu](http://In1.Cu)

The first internal layer is mainly a **ground plane**.

A large, mostly uninterrupted ground plane gives signals on the top layer a nearby return path.

### Layer 3 — [In2.Cu](http://In2.Cu)

The second internal layer is also mainly **ground**.

This gives signals routed on the bottom layer a nearby ground reference and helps maintain a continuous ground structure through the board.

### Layer 4 — [B.Cu](http://B.Cu)

The bottom layer is used for additional routing and a large **3.3 V copper pour**.

Vias assigned to the 3.3 V net connect into this copper area, allowing power to be distributed around the PCB without routing a separate long trace to every device.

A simplified view is:

**[F.Cu](http://F.Cu) — components and signals**  
**[In1.Cu](http://In1.Cu) — GND**  
**[In2.Cu](http://In2.Cu) — GND**  
**[B.Cu](http://B.Cu) — 3.3 V distribution and signals**

## Why Ground Planes Matter

One of the most useful concepts I learned was that signals need a **return path**.

Current does not simply travel down a signal trace and disappear. It has to return to its source.

For high-frequency signals, the return current prefers to flow through the nearby ground plane underneath the signal trace.

That means a top-layer trace and the ground plane underneath it work together.

This is especially important for RF and other fast signals.

Keeping the ground plane continuous gives the return current a short path and helps reduce noise and unwanted electromagnetic interference.

## What Vias Actually Do

Vias connect copper between PCB layers.

For example, a 3.3 V connection can go:

**MCU power pin → copper trace → via → bottom 3.3 V copper**

A ground connection can similarly go:

**component ground → ground via → internal ground plane**

I also learned that vias matter for signal return paths.

When a signal changes from one outer layer to another using a via, its reference plane can also change. Adding a nearby ground via gives the return current a path between the ground planes instead of forcing it to travel around the board.

The tutorial uses ground transfer vias near signal vias specifically to maintain this continuous return path through the vertical layer transition.

## Short and Wide Power Connections

Another lesson was that trace width is not only about whether a trace can safely carry enough DC current.

Narrow, long connections also have more inductance.

For power and ground connections, the tutorial uses wider traces—often approximately the width of the component pad—to reduce inductance.

So I learned to think about:

**short + wide = better for power and ground**

especially around decoupling capacitors and high-current paths.

## Component Placement Comes Before Routing

One mistake I initially expected to make was routing everything immediately after importing the components.

Instead, I learned that good routing starts with good placement.

Critical components are placed first.

The RF section should be compact. Decoupling capacitors should be close to their MCU pins. Crystal circuitry should stay close to the oscillator pins. The regulator should stay near the power entry.

Once the important circuitry is placed properly, routing becomes much easier.

This changed how I thought about PCB design:

**placement is part of the electrical design, not just making the board look organized.**

## The Bluetooth RF Section

The Bluetooth section introduced me to RF PCB design.

The STM32WB's RF output cannot simply be connected to an antenna with any random trace.

The design uses an impedance-matching network and RF filter before reaching the antenna connection.

The RF trace is designed around a **50 Ω characteristic impedance**.

The required trace width depends on the PCB stackup—the copper thickness, dielectric thickness, and dielectric properties all affect the resulting impedance.

For the stackup used in the tutorial, an impedance calculation gave approximately a 0.19 mm trace for a 50 Ω outer-layer RF connection.

This taught me that trace geometry can be part of the circuit itself.

At RF frequencies, a PCB trace is no longer just a wire.

## USB Differential Pair Routing

USB D+ and D− also introduced me to differential signaling.

Instead of treating them as unrelated traces, they are routed together as a pair.

The tutorial targets approximately **90 Ω differential impedance** and adjusts both the trace width and the spacing between the two traces.

Even though the board uses USB Full Speed and the tutorial notes that strict impedance control is less critical for such a short connection, working through the process helped me understand how differential-pair routing is designed.

# 3. PCB

![](/images/uploads/image-6.png)

## Designing to the Manufacturer

Another important lesson was that PCB design rules do not come out of nowhere.

The manufacturer has limits for things such as:

- minimum trace width
- minimum spacing
- drill sizes
- via sizes
- copper thickness
- layer stackup

The PCB should be designed around those manufacturing capabilities rather than pushing every feature to the smallest possible size.

For controlled-impedance traces, the manufacturer should also confirm the final trace dimensions because they know the exact materials and stackup they will fabricate.

## ERC and DRC

I learned two important checks in KiCad.

**ERC — Electrical Rules Check**

This checks the schematic for electrical problems.

**DRC — Design Rules Check**

This checks the PCB layout for physical and routing-rule problems such as incorrect clearances or other design-rule violations.

Running these checks does not automatically guarantee that the hardware is correct, but they catch many easy mistakes before manufacturing.

## Manufacturing Files

The final PCB design is not what the manufacturer directly uses.

The design has to be exported into manufacturing files.

The project generated files such as:

- Gerber files for the individual PCB layers
- drill files for vias and holes
- a Bill of Materials (BOM)
- component-position files for assembly
- manufacturing notes

For a board requiring controlled impedance, the tutorial also prepares notes identifying the 50 Ω single-ended RF trace and the 90 Ω USB differential pair so the manufacturer can verify or adjust the stackup and trace dimensions.

These fabrication, placement, and BOM files are then what can be submitted to the PCB manufacturer for fabrication and assembly.

## The Biggest Things I Learned

This project gave me my first look at the full PCB development process:

**Documentation → schematic → ERC → component selection → footprints → stackup → placement → routing → power/ground design → DRC → manufacturing files**

More importantly, I started understanding *why* PCB layout decisions matter.

A decoupling capacitor is not useful just because it appears on the schematic—it has to be close to the device.

A ground plane is not just unused copper—it provides a return path.

A via is not simply a way to escape a crowded layer—it also changes the path the signal and return current take through the board.

A trace is not always just a wire—at high frequencies its width, spacing, and distance from the ground plane affect its impedance.

And manufacturing is not something that happens after PCB design. The manufacturer's capabilities need to influence the design from the beginning.

For a first PCB project, that was probably my biggest takeaway: **PCB design is a combination of circuit design, physical layout, signal and power integrity, documentation, and manufacturing.**
